subject: Cloud Computing
title: Chaos Engineering
description: A short lesson to help you apply Chaos Engineering.

hook.text: Netflix intentionally breaks its own production systems — during business hours. They call it Chaos Monkey.

buildup.text: Chaos engineering injects failures on purpose to test resilience. Kill a server. Slow the network. See what happens.

discovery.text: It reveals hidden dependencies and assumptions. Systems that seem robust often fail in unexpected ways.

twist.text: Most teams fear breaking things on purpose. But controlled failure tests beat discovering weaknesses during outages.

climax.text: AWS, Google, and Azure all recommend chaos engineering. If you haven't tested failure, you don't know if recovery works.

punchline.text: Break things on purpose. So they don't break by surprise.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of chaos engineering?
options: Deliberately injecting failures to discover weaknesses before real outages occur
Creating random bugs in source code to test developers
Shutting down all services to save cloud costs

details.summary: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures into production systems to verify that resilience mechanisms work as expected. Netflix pioneered the practice with Chaos Monkey. The goal is to find weaknesses before real outages expose them to customers.
details.whyItMatters: Systems that are never tested under failure conditions fail unpredictably when real incidents occur. Chaos engineering builds confidence that recovery mechanisms actually work under pressure.
takeaways: Failures are deliberately injected into production systems
Verifies that resilience mechanisms work as designed
Netflix's Chaos Monkey popularized the practice

faq.question: Is it safe to run chaos experiments in production?
faq.answer: Yes, when done carefully. Start with small blast radius experiments, have rollback procedures ready, and monitor closely. The whole point is to test in production where real conditions exist. Non-production environments often lack the complexity that reveals real weaknesses.

faq.question: What tools are used for chaos engineering?
faq.answer: AWS Fault Injection Simulator, Gremlin, Litmus for Kubernetes, and Netflix's Chaos Monkey are popular tools. They can kill instances, introduce latency, block network traffic, and simulate regional failures in controlled experiments.
